newsitem.title: UK: IIF backs BIS derivatives reporting proposals.
newsitem.headline: IIF backs BIS derivatives reporting proposals.

text.p: The Institute of International Finance (IIF) said on Tuesday it welcomed proposals by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on creating a global reporting framework for derivatives.
The financiers group said in a statement this "would enable the BIS to compile and release statistical aggregates of derivative market activity on a regular and timely basis."

It also said it would be in line with an IIF recommendation that market transparency would be improved if private firms gave more meaningful public disclosures and the official sector compiled and released aggregate market statistics.
But the IIF has reservations about certain details.

The appropriate focus for such a framework should be on aggregate market risks rather than the proposed aggregation of gross market values, which "is not likely to provide meaningful insight into broader macroeconomic trends related to the use of derivative instruments," it said.

"We believe that the imperfections of the proposed framework should be acknowledged and that a commitment to improving the framework should be made," Barbara Matthews, the IIF's banking advisor and regulatory counsel, said.

The IIF also said it strongly supported the proposal in the report that a continuing dialogue should be established between central banks and reporting market participants in order to increase the understanding of both parties concerning techniques for aggregating market risk.

The body, which represents some 230 organisations, including 160 banks, said it also supported the proposed implementation date for the framework, which coincided with new market risk capital adequacy rules for banks coming into force.
But it asked that the issue of the frequency of release of the derivative statistics be clarified quickly.
John Hasletine, the IIF's deputy managing director, told a press briefing in London that the proposals were important in two main respects.

First, they had been drawn up after consultation with industry participants on what sort of statistics should be collected and, second, they recognised the part the BIS committee has in bringing greater transparency to the markets.
